what_it_does: Every chip needs a network of wires to deliver power from the external supply pins to every logic cell — this is called the power distribution network or power grid. At very small feature sizes (below 5 nanometers), modern chips have so many cells that their power grids contain billions or even trillions of connection points, and simulating how voltage drops across this grid requires solving an enormous set of simultaneous equations. A standard approach called domain decomposition splits the grid into subregions and solves each one separately, but the math that couples the subregions together (called the Schur complement) grows so large it becomes the bottleneck. This paper proposes a nested version of domain decomposition that introduces an intermediate coupling step, breaking that bottleneck into smaller, more manageable pieces and parallelizing the Schur complement computation across many processors. The result is a solver that scales to the billion-node grids found in state-of-the-art chips, according to the abstract.
